scribe_response.text: Tell me about a meal or a dish that brings back memories. The dish that brings everything back for me is my mother's chicken adobo. She cooked it on Sundays, on Sundays, when my father came home early from the water. I can still see the black iron pot on the clay stove, its lid rattling. First she crushed a whole head of garlic with the flat of her knife. Then she poured in vinegar and soy sauce, with dried bay leaves and black pepper. The vinegar was made from coconut sap, sharp and a little sweet. She never measured anything, and when I asked how much, she said enough. For years that answer made me furious, um because I wanted to be a good cook. Now I understand that enough is a real measurement, and it lives in your hands. While the chicken simmered, we children hung around the stove like hungry cats. Nestor was the worst, because he uh lifted the lid every five minutes. My mother tapped his fingers with a wooden spoon, and he yelped as if burned. We ate together on the porch, on a long bench my father made from a boat plank. My mother served the rice first, a mountain of it, steaming in, in the um morning light. What happened next? Then um she spooned the dark sauce over the top, and the rice drank it up. There was never enough chicken for everyone, so the sauce was the real treasure. My father always gave me the thigh and winked, as if it uh were our um secret. I think he knew I was the thin one who forgot to eat when reading. Afterward we had sliced green mango with salt, and it made our eyes water happily. The adobo tasted even better the next day, once the flavors had settled. My mother said that was the secret of life, because some things improve when left alone. When I moved to Abu Dhabi, I packed a small bottle of that coconut vinegar. It leaked on my best blue blouse, and the whole airplane smelled like a Filipino kitchen. The um first time I made adobo in my new kitchen, I cried into the pot. It tasted close, but not quite right, because the memory was missing. Ramon laughed and said it was perfect, but he was being kind. Over the years I found the right vinegar in a supermarket near our building. Now my daughter Liza asks for my adobo after every long shift at the, the hospital. Can you tell me more about that? She um sits at my table in her blue uniform and eats three plates in silence. I tell her that is exactly how I looked at my, my mother's table. My son Paolo wants extra sauce and um a fried egg, which, egg which my mother would never allow. I let him, because sons and grandchildren are allowed um things that daughters never were. Sometimes I use a pressure cooker now, and I feel a little guilty. My mother's pot was never in a hurry, and her adobo carried that patience. On tired days I put on the rice and chop the garlic slowly. The smell comes up, and suddenly I am eight years old on that bamboo porch. I can hear the river, the rooster, and my brothers fighting over the last fish. A single dish can carry a whole house inside it, with its people and weather. That is the kind of memory no restaurant can sell you. I believe that is why we um cook for the people we love. When I am gone, I hope my children will stand at the stove and say enough. Then they will smile, and I will be there in the steam.
